headline: The war premium leaks out before the UN
standfirst: Brent traded under $102 this morning and WTI broke $100, a fourth straight losing session and the lowest for both since 10 September, as traders priced a chance of US–Iran contact at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia worked to restore its East–West pipeline. There is no US data today — Chicago Fed's Goolsbee at 06:30 ET is the only scheduled Fed event — so the week's risk sits on Wednesday's flash PMIs and three Treasury auctions into a ten-year that closed Friday at 5.01%.

bullets.title: The oil premium is leaking, and it has not gone
bullets.text: Crude has fallen for four sessions. Brent was down about 2% this morning near $101.7 and WTI broke below $100, both the lowest since 10 September, after Trump said he would "probably" be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, with Qatar passing messages between the two. Saudi Arabia is aiming to restore roughly half its East–West pipeline capacity within days and all of it within six weeks, shuttling crude through the Strait of Hormuz in the meantime; JPMorgan put Middle East flows at 17.1 million barrels a day over the past ten days, still 6.1 million below the 2025 average. Against that, Houthi missiles and drones hit Saudi Arabia on Saturday, Iran has promised "painful" retaliation and Trump says he is in "deciding mode". Brent was about $72 before the war began in late February and near $110 earlier last week.

bullets.title: A ten-year at 5% is now the constraint on everything else
bullets.text: The ten-year closed Friday at 5.01% after touching roughly 5.04% on 15–16 September, its first close above 5% since July 2007, and is on course for a seventh consecutive monthly rise. The thirty-year is 5.34% and the twenty-year 5.38%. The move is a real-yield move, not an inflation-expectations one: ten-year breakevens have risen less than 10bp since the war began against roughly 100bp on real yields. Supply is the other half of the story — the fiscal 2026 deficit is approaching $2 trillion and Treasury has been leaning on bills while raising its 10- to 30-year buybacks to at least $4 billion an operation.

bullets.title: The curve has given up half its slope in a month
bullets.text: The two-year is 4.76% against about 4.24% a month ago; the ten-year is 5.01% against about 4.74%. That takes 2s10s to 25bp from roughly 50bp, and it flattened another 2bp on Friday as the two-year added 9bp to the ten-year's 7bp. 3M10Y is still 87bp positive and widened on the week. A curve flattening while every point on it rises is a hiking cycle being priced, not a recession.

bullets.title: Eight major central banks have moved and the market wants more
bullets.text: The Fed is at 3.75–4.00% after a unanimous 25bp on 16 September, its first hike since 2023. The Bank of Japan went to 1.25% on 18 September, a 31-year high. The ECB is at 2.50% after its second increase of the year, with Governing Council members saying no meeting is ruled out. The Bank of England held at 3.75% on a 6–3 vote and stopped selling long gilts. The Bank of Canada is still at 2.25%, but its minutes said hikes may be needed if high oil prices pass into other goods. Friday's money markets priced another 25bp from the Fed by year-end and two more by June 2027.

bullets.title: The week's real event is supply, and it is not on most calendars
bullets.text: Treasury sells $69 billion of two-years on Tuesday, $70 billion of five-years on Wednesday and $44 billion of seven-years on Thursday, into a curve at its highs. New York Fed President Williams speaks at the Treasury Market Conference on Tuesday. Flash September PMIs land Wednesday: US manufacturing is seen at 53.6 after 53.9 and services at 56.0 after 56.5. With a Fed that has said it wants to see restriction, a strong flash reads hawkish rather than as good news.

calendar.note: A 2027 voter. Warsh has deliberately stopped giving forward guidance, so speeches are the only read on the path between meetings — which makes them carry more than they used to.

calendar.event: ECB President Lagarde and BoC Governor Macklem both speak
calendar.note: Macklem is the one to watch: the Bank of Canada is still at 2.25% with about 59% priced for an October hike, and its September minutes flagged oil pass-through.

calendar.event: UN General Assembly opens in New York
calendar.note: The unscheduled risk. Any signal on a Trump–Pezeshkian meeting trades oil first and everything else second. A Trump–Xi summit is also expected this week.

calendar.event: $69bn two-year auction; Williams at the Treasury Market Conference
calendar.note: The front end is where the repricing has happened. A soft two-year tail would say the market does not believe the dots it just sold off for.

calendar.event: US flash PMIs (September); euro area 04:00, UK 04:30
calendar.note: Manufacturing seen 53.6 after 53.9, services 56.0 after 56.5. The first US data of the week and the first read on activity since the hike.

calendar.event: Jobless claims; new home sales 10:00; SNB decision 03:30
calendar.note: Claims are seen at 202,000 after 196,000. New home sales fell 10.5% last month, with mortgage rates approaching 7%. The SNB is expected to hold at 0%.
Durable goods seen −0.5% after +1.1%. The Michigan one-year inflation expectation, 4.6% in the preliminary, matters more here than the sentiment headline.
The print the Fed named. Core PCE was 3.3% year-over-year last month and the September projections assume 3.4% for the year.

sessionNote: A Monday with no US data and a live geopolitical wire is a headline tape, not a data tape. Friday's levels are the reference: S&P 7,650.50, Dow 51,682.64, Nasdaq 26,522.54. Overnight the pattern that has run all week held — crude down more than 2%, US futures up, with Dow futures about +0.23%, S&P +0.34% and Nasdaq 100 +0.55% late Sunday — and Asia followed, with the Nikkei up 1.38% and the Kospi 1.47%. The clean window is the US morning; the risk is that the move that matters arrives from New York diplomacy rather than from an opening bell.
watchOut: Trading the de-escalation as if it were done. Crude has round-tripped this move twice since February: Brent was near $110 early last week and about $72 before the war. What has actually happened is a possible meeting, a pipeline under repair and a flow number that is still 6.1 million barrels a day below last year's average — set against Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia on Saturday and an Iranian promise of retaliation. A short-energy or long-duration position sized for a settlement is sized for the one outcome nobody has been shown yet.

archive.headline: The hike landed. The bond market blinked first.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The Fed's unanimous 25bp on Wednesday took the Dow down 631 points and Thursday gave most of it back, with the S&P up 1.14% to 7,637.76 as the ten-year fell to 4.93% and oil slid. The weekend risk was the Iran war, with Trump saying he was near a decision on resuming large-scale strikes.

archive.headline: The ten-year touched 5% into the decision. The hike is not the event.
archive.summary: FOMC day. The 10-year had closed at 5.00% after touching 5.04%, the highest since 2007, with a 25bp hike priced at 92–94%. WTI had jumped 5.1% to $106.56 as fighting intensified in the Middle East; every US sector but energy closed red on Tuesday.

archive.headline: Core CPI ran hot into an FOMC that is now 90% priced to hike
archive.summary: Weekend edition. Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected, PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year, and September hike odds moved from 61% to about 90%. Equities closed the week higher regardless — S&P +0.86% Friday, VIX −11% — while the 10-year finished at 4.96%.

archive.headline: Core CPI at a four-month high, hike odds jump to ~90%
archive.summary: Headline CPI held at 3.4% year-over-year but core rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected. Energy added 2.1% and gasoline 3.9%; airline fares rose 2.7%. Equities rallied regardless — S&P +0.86%, VIX −11% — while the 10-year touched 4.97%.

archive.headline: PPI beats, ECB hikes to 2.50%
archive.summary: August PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year against 5.3% expected with July revised up from flat. The ECB raised its deposit rate 25bp to 2.50% effective 16 September and cut its 2028 inflation forecast to 2.1%. September hike odds moved from 61% to 72%.

archive.headline: Oil tops $100, Dow sheds 400 more
archive.summary: Brent broke $100 for the first time since July and the 10-year yield hit a three-year high. Amgen fell over 10% on a failed cardiovascular trial and software names sold off. Barclays nonetheless lifted its year-end S&P target to 7,950.
